claims.text: A CaF2-containing refractory high-entropy-alloy composite can provide self-lubrication over a wide temperature range.
CaF2 is a high-temperature-stable lubricating phase.
Adding CaF2 to a refractory high-entropy-alloy matrix will reduce friction while retaining high mechanical strength.
Refractory high-entropy alloys have excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures.
Spark plasma sintering is suitable for producing dense high-entropy-alloy bulk material.
Spark plasma sintering or high-pressure synthesis can produce an optimized, homogeneous dispersion of CaF2 in a refractory high-entropy-alloy matrix.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale or microscale CaF2 particles can migrate to the sliding interface.
CaF2 particles at the sliding interface form a lubricious tribofilm while coexisting with a mechanically robust matrix.
At elevated temperatures, CaF2 becomes tribologically active and forms a protective lubricating layer.
The CaF2-derived lubricating layer reduces friction and wear.
The refractory high-entropy-alloy matrix can sustain overall strength and high-temperature stability in the CaF2-containing composite.
The composite will have a reduced friction coefficient and wear rate from room temperature to approximately 1000 degrees Celsius.
Optimally dispersed CaF2 will limit the composite's mechanical-strength reduction to approximately 10–20% relative to the unmodified matrix.
The beneficial tribological effect requires homogeneous CaF2 incorporation at an optimal volume fraction.
Excessive CaF2 content will compromise the matrix's mechanical strength.
Insufficient CaF2 content will fail to develop an effective lubricating film.
High-entropy alloys can maintain substantial strength and creep resistance near 982 degrees Celsius.
